Twenty-one participants were excluded prior to analyses: 12 did not pass the training phase, 4 were excluded for not meeting US citizenship criteria, 2 were found to be in the wrong age group, 2 did not consent for their data to be included following completion of the study, and 1 did not follow task instructions.

table.text: Specifically, participants were provided with a detailed explanation of the distinction and then asked to classify three distinct memory descriptions, each depicting either a unique, general, or lifetime period memory.
For each musical cue, participants were presented with the song, the artist's name, and the title of the song for a total of 15 seconds.
Following the presentation of each song, participants were instructed to type a description of their memory.

After providing their description and before moving onto the next musical cue, participants completed a categorical rating indicating the level of specificity of the memory (i.e., unique, general, or lifetime period) and then completed a set of phenomenological ratings.

At the conclusion of the study, participants were asked whether they were attending high school, university, or outside of university (i.e., early adulthood) in the years corresponding to the musical cues used in the study.
The resulting exceedance probabilities therefore represent the estimated likelihood that participants provided a rating above 1.
In fact, participants were most likely to report lifetime period memories (M = 0.51, SD = 0.26), followed by unique (M = 0.26, SD = 0.20) and general events (M = 0.23, SD = 0.23).
This demonstrates that, in most cases, when participants were categorizing their memories as general events or lifetime periods, they were not thinking about any related unique events.

Sixteen participants were excluded prior to analyses: 5 were excluded for failing the training phase, 3 were excluded for not meeting the citizenship criterion, 3 were identified as being in the wrong age group, 4 did not comply with instructions, and 1 did not consent for their data to be included following completion of the study.
First, on each trial, participants were instructed to indicate whether any unique events came to mind whenever they reported general and lifetime period memories (yes/no).

Second, because the results of Study 1 indicated that the timing of the categorical specificity rating did not influence the proportion of unique events reported by participants, the categorical memory specificity ratings in Study 2 were always made immediately after participants provided the memory description.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants were 35-, 45-, and 55-year-old Americans who were recruited through the Prolific research platform. The pre-registered sample size was based on power analyses of previous studies of musically-evoked autobiographical memories that: (i) included age and/or life stage as design factors, (ii) included specificity and/or MTT as a dependent variable (DV), and (iii) reported relevant effect sizes. Cady et al. (2008) examined the effect of life stage on memory specificity and MTT, reporting large effect sizes for both DVs (ηp² = 0.36 and 0.18, respectively). Jakubowski et al. (2023) examined the effect of age on memory specificity, reporting a medium effect size (ηp² = 0.07). Given the novelty of the research question addressed in the present study, G*Power version 3.1 was used to estimate the required sample size using the weakest relevant effect reported in the literature, i.e., a medium effect of ηp² = 0.07. This analysis indicated that a total sample size of N = 168 (or 56 participants per group) was needed to provide sufficient power (0.95) to detect a main effect in a mixed ANOVA. To account for up to 20% attrition (i.e., participants who do not consent to include their data in the final sample and participants who do not complete the survey with usable responses), we planned to collect data from a total of 201 participants (or 67 per condition). In total, 207 participants (N35 = 69, N45 = 67, N55 = 71) participated in Mental Time Travel 8 the study. Slightly higher counts were obtained for the 35-and 55-year-old cohorts due to automated platform buffers in Prolific for active submissions. Twenty-one participants were excluded prior to analyses: 12 did not pass the training phase, 4 were excluded for not meeting US citizenship criteria, 2 were found to be in the wrong age group, 2 did not consent for their data to be included following completion of the study, and 1 did not follow task instructions. This left a final sample of 186 participants (N35 = 59, N45 = 63, and N55 = 64; for demographic details, see Supplemental Materials).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Music, Memory, and Mental Time Travel
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Participants will describe memories and make phenomenological ratings in response to musical cues that are related to three distinct lifetime periods (high school, university/college, and young adulthood; 4 songs per lifetime period).

We will vary the age of participants (35, 45, or 55 years old) and, as noted above, the lifetime period during which various pieces of music were popular (high school [age 15], university/college [age 20] and young adulthood [age 25]).

Specificity:
(1) Based on existing research, we expect that approximately 50% of reported memories will refer to specific events and the other 50% will refer to general events and/or lifetime periods.
(2) Age: We expect fewer specific events as a function of increasing age.
(3) Lifetime period: We expect fewer specific events for lifetime periods that are further back in time.

Mental time travel (MTT):
We expect MTT to be present for memories at all levels of specificity. We further expect MTT to be stronger for specific than general memories (Ford et al., 2011), but also for MTT for non-specific events (general, lifetime period) to be significantly above the bottom point of the rating scale provided to participants.
table.design_dependent_variables:
The two primary DVs will be (i) the level of specificity of memories and (ii) the extent to which each memory is associated with MTT.

Level of specificity will be measured by asking participants to indicate whether each reported memory reflects a specific event, general event, or lifetime period.

MTT will be measured using three 7-point rating scales that relate to three core features of the concept, i.e., projection, re-experience, and re-feeling.
table.study_design_overview: The mixed 3 (Participant age: 35, 45, or 55 years old; between subjects) x 3 (Life stage: high school, university/college, and young adulthood; within subjects) design will result in 9 conditions.
table.statistical_tests:
Analyses (one for each DV) will be carried out using mixed effects models that account for the nested structure of the data. Age and Life Stage will be treated as fixed effects and Participant will be treated as a random effect.

In order to assess whether MTT is above the bottom point of the rating scale (i.e., 1 = not at all) for specific events, general events, and lifetime periods, we will run a cumulative link mixed model that can account for both the nested structure and ordinal nature of the data and that will allow us to estimate the log odds of MTT ratings being above a predefined threshold (i.e., 1 = not at all). 

All analyses will be carried out using JASP software.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Prior to beginning the study, participants will receive detailed instructions about the distinctions between unique events, general events, and lifetime periods. They will then have two opportunities to answer questions demonstrating that they have learned these distinctions. Any participant who does not demonstrate that they have learned this distinction after two attempts to answer questions will not proceed to complete the study.

There will be two attention check trials during the study during which participants will be asked to select a particular value on a rating scale. Any participant who fails both attention checks will be excluded from data analysis.

At the conclusion of the study, participants will be asked to indicate the years in which they attended high school and university/college. Any participant for whom the songs presented did not align with their time in either high school, university/college, and young adulthood (defined as post-university) will be excluded from analyses. This will help us to ensure that our stimuli were targeting the life stages of interest.

Any participant who responds to all rating scales using one response option, suggesting lack of engagement with the task, will be excluded from analyses.

Any participant who generates task non-compliant descriptions of memories will be excluded.
table.sample_size: Our sample size was determined on the basis of power analyses of previous studies of musically-evoked autobiographical memories that: (i) included age and/or life stage as design factors, (ii) included specificity and/or MTT as a DV, and (iii) reported relevant effect sizes. Cady et al. (2008) examined the effect of life stage on memory specificity and MTT, reporting large effect sizes for both DVs (partial eta squared = 0.36 and 0.18, respectively). Jakubowski et al. (2023) examined the effect of age on memory specificity, reporting a medium effect size (partial eta squared = 0.07). Given the novelty of the research question that we are addressing in our study, we used G*Power version 3.1 to estimate our sample size using the weakest relevant effect reported in the literature, i.e., a medium effect of  partial eta squared = 0.07. This analysis revealed that a total sample size of N = 168 (or 56 participants per group) is needed to provide sufficient power (0.95) to detect a main effect in a mixed ANOVA. In order to account for up to 20% attrition (i.e., participants who do not consent to include their data in the final sample and participants who do not complete the survey with usable responses [see Outliers and Exclusion above]), we will collect data from 201 participants (or 67 per condition).
table.additional_comments:
In addition to specificity and ratings of MTT, we will also ask participants to complete four 7-point rating scales related to the perceptual, conceptual, idiosyncratic, and shared details that will allow us to map them onto a novel multidimensional model of mental representations (Addis & Szpunar, 2024). Participants will also complete an additional seven 7-point rating scales related to detail, positive valence, negative valence, emotional intensity, familiarity, effort, and previous thinking that will allow us to situate our findings in the larger literature on music and memory. 

Most ratings (e.g., MTT, perceptual, conceptual, idiosyncratic, and shared content) will be completed immediately after each memory is described by the participant. The specificity ratings will be completed either immediately after memory descriptions (as with other ratings) or after all memories have been described and rated on the various other phenomenological characteristics. The purpose of manipulating the timing of the specificity rating will be to assess whether having participants rate specificity right after describing their memories influences the likelihood of reporting specific, general, or lifetime period memories. We do not expect this manipulation to impact the results but will use the data as a basis for future investigations should the manipulation turn out to be significant.

table.title: Music, Memory, and Mental Time Travel (Study 2)
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
The purpose of this study is to replicate and extend the findings from an initial study that revealed the presence of mental time travel (MTT) across all levels of memory specificity. The current study will use a new set of musical cues to account for the fact that the study is taking place approximately one year after the first study. The current study will also more thoroughly assess the presence/absence of specific memories, even when participants report general and lifetime period memories (see below).

Participants will describe memories and make phenomenological ratings in response to musical cues that are related to three distinct lifetime periods (high school, university/college, and young adulthood; 4 songs per lifetime period).

We will vary the age of participants (35, 45, or 55 years old) and, as noted above, the lifetime period during which various pieces of music were popular (high school [age 15], university/college [age 20] and young adulthood [age 25]).

Specificity:
Based on the results of Study 1, we expect that approximately 50% of reported memories will refer to lifetime period memories.
Age: We expect fewer specific events as a function of increasing age.
Lifetime period: Based on the results of Study 1, we do not expect a main effect of lifetime period on ratings of specificity (i.e., no differences in specificity ratings across memories from high school, university, and young adulthood).

Mental time travel (MTT):
We expect MTT to be present for memories at all levels of specificity. We further expect MTT to be stronger for specific than general memories (Ford et al., 2011), but also for MTT for non-specific events (general, lifetime period) to be significantly above the bottom point of the rating scale provided to participants. Lastly, the current study will more thoroughly assess whether participants might have any specific memories associated with their general and lifetime period memories (see below). We expect MTT to be present for general and lifetime period memories irrespective of whether those memories are associated with specific memories.
table.design_dependent_variables:
The two primary DVs will be (i) the level of specificity of memories and (ii) the extent to which each memory is associated with MTT.

Level of specificity will be measured by asking participants to indicate whether each reported memory reflects a specific event, general event, or lifetime period. In cases where participants indicate that a memory reflects a general event or lifetime period, they will additionally be asked to indicate whether any specific event came to mind while thinking about the memory. 

MTT will be measured using three 7-point rating scales that relate to three core features of the concept, i.e., projection, re-experience, and re-feeling.

All analyses will be carried out using R software.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Prior to beginning the study, participants will receive detailed instructions about the distinctions between unique events, general events, and lifetime periods. They will then have two opportunities to answer questions demonstrating that they have learned these distinctions. As in Study 1, we also aim to account for up to 20% attrition by collecting data from a total of 201 participants (67 per between-subjects condition).

As in Study 1, life stage did not predict the proportion of unique Mental Time Travel 17 events, b = -0.02, t(355.4) = -1.03, p = .306, β = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.06] (high school: M = 0.32, SE = 0.02; college/university: M = 0.22, SE = 0.02; young adulthood: M = 0.29, SE = 0.02).

live_data_statements: First, participants provided higher ratings of re-living for specific events than general events and lifetime periods, supporting the close association of MTT to episodic memory.
Participants were 35-, 45-, and 55-year-old Americans who were recruited through the Prolific research platform.
Slightly higher counts were obtained for the 35-and 55-year-old cohorts due to automated platform buffers in Prolific for active submissions.

Twenty-one participants were excluded prior to analyses: 12 did not pass the training phase, 4 were excluded for not meeting US citizenship criteria, 2 were found to be in the wrong age group, 2 did not consent for their data to be included following completion of the study, and 1 did not follow task instructions.
Participants completed the study online as a Qualtrics survey that was delivered to them using the Prolific platform.
Additionally, participants had to pass the specificity training described below, and at least one of two attention checks.
Participants were then trained to differentiate between unique, general, and lifetime period memories (Ford et al., 2011).

Specifically, participants were provided with a detailed explanation of the distinction and then asked to classify three distinct memory descriptions, each depicting either a unique, general, or lifetime period memory.
For each musical cue, participants were presented with the song, the artist's name, and the title of the song for a total of 15 seconds.
Following the presentation of each song, participants were instructed to type a description of their memory.

After providing their description and before moving onto the next musical cue, participants completed a categorical rating indicating the level of specificity of the memory (i.e., unique, general, or lifetime period) and then completed a set of phenomenological ratings.

At the conclusion of the study, participants were asked whether they were attending high school, university, or outside of university (i.e., early adulthood) in the years corresponding to the musical cues used in the study.
The resulting exceedance probabilities therefore represent the estimated likelihood that participants provided a rating above 1.
In fact, participants were most likely to report lifetime period memories (M = 0.51, SD = 0.26), followed by unique (M = 0.26, SD = 0.20) and general events (M = 0.23, SD = 0.23).
This demonstrates that, in most cases, when participants were categorizing their memories as general events or lifetime periods, they were not thinking about any related unique events.

First, on each trial, participants were instructed to indicate whether any unique events came to mind whenever they reported general and lifetime period memories (yes/no).

text.text: The subjective sense of mentally reliving the past is considered the key distinguishing feature of episodic memory-a neurocognitive system supporting recollection of specific life events.

We present data from two pre-registered studies of musically-evoked autobiographical memory demonstrating that this subjective sense of mental reliving accompanies not just memories for specific events, but also more general autobiographical representations.
Groups of 35-, 45-, and 55-year-old participants reported memories in response to musical cues that had been popular during their time in high-school, university, and early adulthood.
Participants also rated the level of specificity and sense of mental time travel associated with each memory.
Cumulative link mixed model analyses revealed that participants endorsed the presence of the subjective sense of mental time travel for specific, general, and lifetime period memories.
Implication of reliving broader swaths of the personal past are discussed in relation to theories of episodic and autobiographical memory.
A familiar song, a distinct scent, or an old photograph can sometimes make the present moment give way to the past in a way that transports people to an earlier point in their life.

Cognitive psychologists metaphorically refer to this subjective sense of displacement as mental time travel (MTT), which has become closely associated with the concept of episodic memory-the capacity to remember events that occurred in a specific time and place, such as a first kiss or a car accident.

Episodic memory was introduced as a heuristic distinction from shared knowledge of the world (i.e., semantic memory; Tulving, 1972), however, it was subsequently developed into a theory of a distinct neurocognitive system (Tulving, 1983 (Tulving, , 2002 (Tulving, , 2005)).

text.text: On this later account, episodic memory does not merely provide information about what events occurred in the past.
It allows the individual to become consciously aware of a prior experience as part of their own personal past.
This formulation has shaped decades of research on remembering past events.
Yet, as we argue below, the theory of episodic memory has positioned the concept of MTT in a way that obscures its possible role in non-specific representations of the past (Addis & Szpunar, 2024).

text.text: In addition, Tulving developed the remember/know paradigm to assess whether people with intact episodic memory could remember the moment in which they were presented specific laboratory stimuli, such as words from a list, or whether they only knew that information had been presented (Gardiner, 1988; Rajaram, 1993).

text.text: Indeed, experimenters now commonly ask participants to rate feelings of being projected into the past when reflecting on memories of events (Zaman et al., 2024) or probe the recapitulation of the original sensoryperceptual context assumed to underpin feelings of re-experiencing (Levine et al., 2002).

text.text: Critically, these various approaches to studying the role of conscious experience in memory have mostly overlooked the possibility that MTT may also be present when people reflect on non-specific memories of their past.

In contrast to traditional laboratory inquiries into memory for events, research on autobiographical memory focuses on how complex, self-relevant life experiences are framed, organized, and functionally applied across the lifespan (Bluck, 2003; McAdams, 2001).

text.text: Autobiographical memories span both specific and conceptual aspects of experience.

According to Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000), knowledge about the personal past is represented hierarchically across different levels of abstraction, including lifetime periods, general events, and event-specific knowledge.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000)</ref>, knowledge about the personal past is represented hierarchically across different levels of abstraction, including lifetime periods, general events, and event-specific knowledge.

text.text: Lifetime periods organize broad stretches of experience (e.g., one's time in high school), general events represent repeated experiences (e.g., daily commutes to and from school), and event-specific knowledge captures isolated elements of prior experience (e.g., receiving one's diploma).

Notably, they initially conceptualized eventspecific knowledge as a summary record of sensory-perceptual processing that could, in combination with memory for general events, evoke an episodic-like memory of repeated experiences accompanied by a sense of MTT.

As further testament to the broad impact of episodic theory on the field of memory research, Conway later reconceptualized event-specific knowledge as episodic memory, rendering the subjective experience of MTT to only the lowest level of the autobiographical knowledge base (Conway, 2005).

text.text: Against this backdrop, autobiographical memory provides a useful testbed for evaluating the possible role of MTT in broader representations of the personal past.
If MTT is unique to episodic memory, then autobiographical representations of lifetime periods or general events should not, on their own, evoke the experience.

Yet, lifetime periods and general events both locate the self in time (Addis & Tippett, 2008; Prebble et al., 2013), which invites the question: Do individuals experience a sense of MTT when reflecting on less specific representations of their personal past?

text.text: As we alluded to earlier, memory researchers have not yet fully addressed such questions because of the assumption that MTT is strictly the domain of episodic memory and thus only occurs when retrieving specific events.
As a departure from this tradition, we set out to investigate whether people can feel transported to a broader period or general event from their past without recollecting a specific event.
Mental Time Travel 5
Music provides a way to test for the presence of MTT in broader representations of the personal past.
Familiar songs are potent cues for remembering autobiographical memories from across the lifespan (e.g., Schulkind et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Familiar songs are potent cues for remembering autobiographical memories from across the lifespan (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Schulkind et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, musical cues do not restrict retrieval to one level of specificity.

Music is often embedded in daily experiences, recurring activities, and extended phases of life, and musically-evoked autobiographical memories commonly remind people of routines and lifetime periods (Jakubowski & Ghosh, 2021; Janata et al., 2007; Schulkind et al., 1999;  for related discussion, see Tanberg et al., 2025).

text.text: Nonetheless, surprisingly few studies have assessed the extent to which musically-evoked autobiographical memories are associated with a subjective sense of MTT (e.g., Cady et al., 2008), and only one study of which we are aware asked participants to provide ratings of MTT in response to musically-evoked memories that referred to lifetime periods, general or repeated experiences, and specific events. Ford et al. (2011) asked participants to indicate the extent to which they were able to re-live or "place themselves back" in response to memories evoked by popular songs.

(2011)</ref> asked participants to indicate the extent to which they were able to re-live or "place themselves back" in response to memories evoked by popular songs.

text.text: Two findings are noteworthy.
First, participants provided higher ratings of re-living for specific events than general events and lifetime periods, supporting the close association of MTT to episodic memory.
However, participants also reported a sense of re-living general and lifetime period memories, albeit to a lesser degree, suggesting that MTT may not be unique to episodic memory.
The data reported by Ford et al. (2011) hold important implications for the central tenet of episodic memory theory, yet those findings have been largely overlooked since their publication.

text.text: Across two pre-registered studies (N = 370), we systematically examined, across different age groups, life stages, musical cues, and behavioural indices of MTT, whether musically-evoked memories of unique events, general events, and lifetime periods are each accompanied by a subjective sense of mentally travelling back in time.

text.text: Study 1 made use of a 3 (Participant age: 35, 45, or 55 years old; between subjects) x 3 (Life stage: high school, university/college, and young adulthood; within subjects) mixed design that resulted in Mental Time Travel 7 'life stages' and the memories that broadly reflect these different stages as 'lifetime period memories' to avoid using the term 'lifetime period' to refer to both the independent and dependent variable.

Stimuli for each condition were excerpts of the four most popular songs (as indexed from the Billboard 100 Charts) from the year in which the participant was assumed to be living through a particular life stage (i.e., high school, university/college, and early adulthood) (for details, see Supplemental Materials).

Each song was 15-seconds in length and contained the most popular melody or lyrics associated with the song, which prior research has indicated provides participants with a sufficient representation of the song as well as enough time to retrieve a memory associated with the musical cue (e.g., Janata et al., 2007; Krumhansl & Zupnick, 2013).

text.text: Participants were 35-, 45-, and 55-year-old Americans who were recruited through the Prolific research platform.

The pre-registered sample size was based on power analyses of previous studies of musically-evoked autobiographical memories that: (i) included age and/or life stage as design factors, (ii) included specificity and/or MTT as a dependent variable (DV), and (iii) reported relevant effect sizes. Cady et al. (2008) examined the effect of life stage on memory specificity and MTT, reporting large effect sizes for both DVs (ηp² = 0.36 and 0.18, respectively). Jakubowski et al. (2023) examined the effect of age on memory specificity, reporting a medium effect size (ηp² = 0.07).

text.text: Given the novelty of the research question addressed in the present study, G*Power version 3.1 was used to estimate the required sample size using the weakest relevant effect reported in the literature, i.e., a medium effect of ηp² = 0.07.
This analysis indicated that a total sample size of N = 168 (or 56 participants per group) was needed to provide sufficient power (0.95) to detect a main effect in a mixed ANOVA.

To account for up to 20% attrition (i.e., participants who do not consent to include their data in the final sample and participants who do not complete the survey with usable responses), we planned to collect data from a total of 201 participants (or 67 per condition).
In total, 207 participants (N35 = 69, N45 = 67, N55 = 71) participated in Mental Time Travel 8 the study.
Slightly higher counts were obtained for the 35-and 55-year-old cohorts due to automated platform buffers in Prolific for active submissions.

Twenty-one participants were excluded prior to analyses: 12 did not pass the training phase, 4 were excluded for not meeting US citizenship criteria, 2 were found to be in the wrong age group, 2 did not consent for their data to be included following completion of the study, and 1 did not follow task instructions.
This left a final sample of 186 participants (N35 = 59, N45 = 63, and N55 = 64; for demographic details, see Supplemental Materials).
Participants completed the study online as a Qualtrics survey that was delivered to them using the Prolific platform.
To assure data authenticity, we included a CAPTCHA test, and disabled copy and paste functions to prevent participants from directly pasting content generated using AI.
Additionally, participants had to pass the specificity training described below, and at least one of two attention checks.

Participants began by providing consent and completing a demographic questionnaire that included information about age, gender/sex, ethnicity, citizenship, and length of residency in the United States prior to beginning the study.
We asked about United States residency as a proxy for exposure to the top US-charting songs during the life stages studied.
Participants were then trained to differentiate between unique, general, and lifetime period memories (Ford et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Participants were then trained to differentiate between unique, general, and lifetime period memories <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Ford et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, participants were provided with a detailed explanation of the distinction and then asked to classify three distinct memory descriptions, each depicting either a unique, general, or lifetime period memory.
Participants who failed the test were provided with an additional opportunity to re-study the distinction and then to classify a new set of three memories.
Any participant who failed both attempts was dismissed from the study.
This training session helped to ensure that participants who completed the study were able to clearly differentiate between unique, general, and lifetime period memories.
Participants who continued onto the study were then tasked with listening to a total of 12 musical cues presented in random order that were popular during three different life stages.
For each musical cue, participants were presented with the song, the artist's name, and the title of the song for a total of 15 seconds.
They were then asked to think of the first memory that came to mind in relation to the song.
They could not advance to the following page of the survey until the full time had elapsed to ensure that they had taken the time to listen to the song and think of a relevant memory.
Following the presentation of each song, participants were instructed to type a description of their memory.

After providing their description and before moving onto the next musical cue, participants completed a categorical rating indicating the level of specificity of the memory (i.e., unique, general, or lifetime period) and then completed a set of phenomenological ratings.

For present purposes, the most relevant phenomenological ratings probed the key features of the concept of MTT: projection, re-experiencing, and re-feeling (1 = not at all;7 = very much) (Rubin et al., 2003; Rubin et al., 2019).

text.text: In addition to these ratings, participants also completed additional exploratory phenomenological ratings (i.e., overall detail, perceptual detail, conceptual detail, idiosyncrasy, shared content, positive and negative affect, emotional intensity, familiarity with the song, effort, and prior thinking associated with each reported memory).
Although we made no predictions in relation to these additional ratings, we present descriptive statistics in the Supplemental Materials for completeness.

As we were interested in the proportion of unique, general, and lifetime period memories, as well as the extent to which memories of differing specificity would be associated with MTT, we counterbalanced whether the categorical specificity ratings were completed immediately after describing each event and before the phenomenological ratings or after completing the study and then returning to the memory descriptions to provide the categorical specificity ratings.
This manipulation allowed us to ensure that providing the categorical specificity ratings during the study did not alter the likelihood of reporting unique, general, or lifetime period memories.

At the conclusion of the study, participants were asked whether they were attending high school, university, or outside of university (i.e., early adulthood) in the years corresponding to the musical cues used in the study.

We note that these data turned out to be more varied than we had anticipated, likely due to the fact that many people do not follow a canonical life path (e.g., some people do not go to high school right after elementary or middle school; some people do not go to university right after high school; some people take longer than four years to graduate university; and so on).
Accordingly, we did not use this data as an exclusion criterion.

Rather, we assumed that various changes that people are likely Mental Time Travel 10 to experience over the course of five years (the time between songs for different life stages), such as those involving where they live, who they socialize with, where they work, and so on, would be enough to bring about distinct life stages and lifetime period memories associated with those stages.
Indeed, as we elaborate on below, lifetime period memories were the most common category of memory reported in the study.

The four dependent variables of particular interest were the categorical rating of memory specificity (i.e., unique, general, or lifetime period) and the 7-point ratings of MTT phenomenology (i.e., amount of projection, re-experiencing, and re-feeling) associated with the reported memories.

Note that although our preregistration stated we would use JASP to carry out data analyses, it turned out that R was better suited to handle the cumulative link mixed models (CLMMs) we used to account for the ordinal nature of the phenomenological rating data.
Accordingly, all analyses were carried out using R (Version 4.5.3; R Core Team, 2022).

We anticipated that unique events would make up approximately 50% of reported memories and that memory specificity would vary as a function of age and life stage, such that increasing age and time since a particular life stage would be associated with fewer memories of unique events.

The lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2015) was used to fit a linear mixed model (LMMs) examining the proportion of specific events, with age group and life stage as fixed effects, and a random intercept per participant.

This was done using the first ordinal threshold, separating ratings of 1 ('not at all') from ratings of 2-7.
The resulting exceedance probabilities therefore represent the estimated likelihood that participants provided a rating above 1.

One possible explanation as to why ratings of MTT are so prominent for general and lifetime period memories is that participants may have remembered episodic memories in the context of reflecting on routines and eras from their lives.
To address this possibility, we carried out an additional analysis that was not preregistered.
Specifically, we had two research assistants independently rate whether each memory description alluded to some semblance of a unique event.
One rater was aware of participants' categorical memory specificity ratings, whereas the other rater was blind to these ratings.
Inter-rater agreement was substantial (Cohen's κ = .62, p < .001, agreement = 85.6%).

text.text: Given the high level of agreement, we used only the blind rater's coding for subsequent analyses.
Of the memories that participants labeled as either general events or lifetime periods, only 18.5% were coded by the rater as alluding to some semblance of a unique event.
This demonstrates that, in most cases, when participants were categorizing their memories as general events or lifetime periods, they were not thinking about any related unique events.
The results demonstrate that unique events evoke a strong sense of MTT, but also that MTT is present in relation to memories of general events and lifetime periods.
These data were consistent irrespective of participant age, life stage, or index of MTT.
Content analyses indicated that most general and lifetime period memories did not, in fact, allude to a unique event, suggesting that MTT may play a broader role in memory than previously thought.
However, it is possible that participants retrieved episodic memories in relation to general and lifetime period memories but did not mention those memories in their descriptions.

To address this possibility, we conducted an additional study that followed the same procedures as Study 1, but that asked participants to indicate whether any unique events came to mind whenever they reported general and lifetime period memories.

text.text: The design of Study 2 was identical to that of Study 1 but made use of a novel set of musical stimuli to account for the fact that Study 2 was run approximately one year after Study 1 (for details, see Supplemental Materials).
Participants were 35-, 45-, and 55-year-old Americans recruited through the Prolific research platform.
We aimed to collect the same number of participants as in Study 1 (N = 201 participants; 67 per condition).
In total, 200 participants (N35 = 67, N45 = 67, N55 = 66) took part in the study.

Sixteen participants were excluded prior to analyses: 5 were excluded for failing the training phase, 3 were excluded for not meeting the citizenship criterion, 3 were identified as being in the wrong age group, 4 did not comply with instructions, and 1 did not consent for their data to be included following completion of the study.
This resulted in a sample of 184 participants (N35 = 62, N45 = 64, and N55 = 58; for demographic details, see Supplemental Materials).
The procedure for Study 2 was identical to that of Study 1, with the following exceptions.
First, on each trial, participants were instructed to indicate whether any unique events came to mind whenever they reported general and lifetime period memories (yes/no).

Second, because the results of Study 1 indicated that the timing of the categorical specificity rating did not influence the proportion of unique events reported by participants, the categorical memory specificity ratings in Study 2 were always made immediately after participants provided the memory description.
Our predictions were identical to that of Study 1, with the following exceptions.
Based on the results of Study 1, we expected that lifetime period memories, as opposed to unique events, would make up approximately 50% of reported memories.
Moreover, we expected that memory specificity would vary as a function of age, but not life stage.
Finally, we anticipated that MTT would be evident at all levels of memory specificity, including general and lifetime period memories for which participants reported no residual episodic memories.
Our approaches to data analysis were identical to that of Study 1.
For each participant, we computed the proportion of unique, general, and lifetime period memories.
Consistent with our prediction, memories most often referred to lifetime periods (M = 0.49, SD = 0.25), followed by unique (M = 0.29, SD = 0.22) and general events (M = 0.22, SD = 0.22).

A onesample t-test showed that the proportion of lifetime period memories did not significantly differ from 50%, t(183) = -0.59, p = .553, d = -0.04, 95% CI [0.45, 0.53], confirming that approximately half of the memories reported were lifetime period memories.
Next, we tested whether the proportion of unique events differed as a function of participant age and life stage.

Unlike Study 1, the proportion of unique events did not decline with participant age, b = -0.001, t(177.7) = -0.04, p = .967, β = -0.004, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.17] (M35 = 0.30, SE35 = 0.03; M45 = 0.23, SE45 = 0.03; M55 = 0.30, SE55 = 0.03).

As in Study 1, life stage did not predict the proportion of unique Mental Time Travel 17 events, b = -0.02, t(355.4) = -1.03, p = .306, β = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.06] (high school: M = 0.32, SE = 0.02; college/university: M = 0.22, SE = 0.02; young adulthood: M = 0.29, SE = 0.02).
In line with predictions, and replicating the results of Study 1, our analyses revealed differences in MTT across all three categories of memory specificity.

text.text: Replicating the results of Study 1, these data support the notion that memories of general events and lifetime periods evoke a subjective sense of MTT.

Participants reported that approximately 25% of general events and 30% of lifetime period memories were associated with a unique memory that came to mind as they were reflecting on the routine or era from their past.

In order to rule out the possibility that the presence of unique memories in the context of reflecting on general and lifetime period memories was driving the sense of MTT associated with these broader memory representations, we carried out the same MTT analyses focusing on the probability of scoring above the bottom point of the rating scale but only including the general and lifetime period memories that were not associated with any residual episodic memory.

These analyses confirmed that ratings of projection, re-experiencing, and re-feeling were all significantly above the scale minimum for both general and lifetime period memories when no residual episodic memories were recalled (all ps < .001).

text.text: Our findings challenge prevailing assumptions about MTT that are deeply rooted in episodic theory.

Whereas episodic theory situates MTT as the quintessential feature of retrieval from episodic memory (Tulving, 1983 (Tulving, , 2002 (Tulving, , 2005)), the data reported here indicate that people also commonly experience a sense of projection, re-experiencing, and re-feeling when reflecting on memories that span broader aspects of their personal past.

text.text: This pattern emerged irrespective of the age of the participant, the life stage under consideration, the musical cue used to evoke the memory, the index of MTT, and whether memories for general events and lifetime periods were accompanied by residual episodic memory.

text.text: However, such approaches perpetuate a dichotomy assuming that MTT is unique to episodic memory.
As a result, researchers rarely measure whether people experience MTT when recalling lifetime periods.

On the contrary, the data reported here indicate that memories of lifetime periods, and general events, constitute rich, affectively laden configurations of self-knowledge that can evoke a distinct past state of being.
These data raise novel questions.
For instance, consider the sense of feeling what it felt like to be oneself in the context of a past lifetime period (for relevant discussion, see Mac Cumhaill, 2020).
What is the nature of this affective state?

Future studies will need to delimit whether the subjective sense of refeeling is associated with particular features or combinations of features of lifetime periods, such as people and places (e.g., Thomsen, 2015; see also, Rubin et al., 2019); the extent to which it is necessary for the stimuli that evoke these feelings to be repeatedly paired with features of lifetime periods over the course of experience; and how such feelings may be abstracted over time.

text.text: Second, the nature of the cuing method will also be important to consider in future work.
For instance, images, food, and other stimuli, much like music, have been shown to evoke a sense of the personal past (e.g., Jakubowski et al., 2023).

text.text: Whether these various classes of cues evoke a sense of MTT in relation to specific and nonspecific aspects of the personal past remains an open question (for philosophical considerations, see Mac Cumhaill, 2020).
It will also be important to consider the functional implications of broadening the concept of MTT to include both specific and non-specific representations of the personal past.

The notion that people do not simply know about their non-specific past but are also able to re-experience it invites questions as to how these phenomenological experiences support various functions that are commonly associated with autobiographical memory, including those related to identity, interactions with others, and behavior (e.g., Harris et al., 2014;  for related discussion, see Stephan & Sedikides, 2024).

text.text: The concept of MTT has played a critical role in positioning episodic memory as a unique neurocognitive system, both in relation to the types of memory seen in other species and the various ways in which humans reflect on the past.
Yet, a growing body of literature challenges the unique nature of episodic memory.

Comparative psychologists continue to demonstrate the highly proficient capabilities for species other than human beings to act on the contents of memories for specific experiences (e.g., Collaro et al., 2024) and cognitive neuroscientists continue to discover strikingly similar neural correlates associated with episodic and semantic memory (e.g., Tibon et al., 2026).

text.text: The data presented here suggest that the subjective sense of revisiting the past extends beyond specific events to encompass the broader rhythms and periods of our lives.

text.text: Phenomenology Questions Variable Description Projection As you were listening to this song, to what extent did you experience a sense of being projected back into the past?
Re-experience As you were listening to this song, to what extent did you experience a sense of re-experiencing the past?
Re-feeling As you were listening to this song, to what extent did you experience a sense of feeling what it felt like to be you in the past?
Perceptual To what extent is your memory characterized by perceptual details such as visual, auditory, or other sensory elements?
Conceptual To what extent is your memory characterized by conceptual details reflecting general knowledge or facts about yourself, your past and/or the world?
Idiosyncratic To what extent is your memory about your own life?
Shared To what extent is your memory about something that others know about or may have experienced themselves?
Detail How detailed is your memory?
